newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks' 91-96 domestic loan losses 42.2 bln Sfr.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks' 91-96 domestic loan losses 42.2 bln Sfr.

text.p: Swiss banks lost a total 42.2 billion Swiss francs on bad domestic loans in the past six years as the country's economy stagnated, the Federal Banking Commission (EBK) said on Tuesday.
The losses represented 8.4 per cent of all domestic credits from 1991 through 1996, according to a survey of 1990s lending risk in Switzerland by the country's banking regulatory agency.
The EBK did not provide a comparative number for earlier years but made clear it viewed the loss level as high.
"Credit risks in domestic business have risen sharply," EBK director Daniel Zuberbuehler told a news conference where the survey was presented.
The EBK said the numbers emerged from its own tally of write-offs, value adjustments and provisions on all categories of domestic loans in the period.
The country's big global banks saw the largest loss levels at 12.5 percent of average loans or 30.1 billion Swiss francs.
Zuberbuehler said this level was reason to question whether international standards for minimum capital coverage of credit risk were high enough.

Swiss credit problems came to a peak last year when the three biggest players -- Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) -- posted first-ever losses after taking huge extraordinary provisions for domestic risks.

The EBK blamed the rising risk on six years of virtually zero economic growth in Switzerland, crumbling corporate credit worthiness and a collapse in the Swiss property market after a boom period in the late 1980s.
The survey covered all categories of Swiss banks, from the biggest global concerns to local savings and loans, and found the highest losses at the largest banks.

Compared to the big banks' level of bad credits, cantonal banks averaged losses of 5.6 percent, regional banks were at 3.9 percent and local Raiffeisenbanken cooperatives had the lowest level at 0.7 percent.
"There are grounds to assume that the out-of-proportion share of losses at the big banks is a reflection of their pronounced policy of expansion in the 1980s," Zuberbuehler said.
Average outstanding domestic loans by all banks from 1991 through 1996 totalled just over 500 billion Swiss francs.

Zuberbuehler said the high percentage figure at big banks raised a question mark over an international standard capital ratio that requires banks to set aside at least eight percent of assets to cover all credit risks.
"Based on this experience, one could demand a rise of the standard capital ratio basis from eight to 10 percent," he said.

But Zuberbuehler made clear he had little hope of winning international support for such a change, which would cost banks money in the short-term by forcing them to set aside more assets for credit coverage.
"At the international level, (changing) the basis of eight percent remains for the moment taboo and can only be done in the medium term at best," he said.

EBK president Kurt Hauri added that he had raised this issue without success for years in the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, an international body of bank regulators who set global standards.
"Switzerland is a small country and the big countries believe that eight percent is not an issue," Hauri said.
The EBK survey included three billion Swiss francs set aside last year by UBS as an extraordinary provision to cover expected losses through 1999.

But the EBK said it did not count about two billion francs each put aside by Credit Suisse Group and SBC in 1996 because these were for long-term potential credit risk, rather than for identified problems that UBS targetted.
